# Lakkhaṇa Sutta (DN 30 (PTS DN iii 142))

**ID:** DN 30 (PTS DN iii 142)
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Lakkhaṇa Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Marks of a Great Man
**PTS:** DN iii 142
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/dn30
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul6.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Lakkhaṇa Sutta* ("The Marks of a Great Man", DN 30) is the thirtieth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Dhammapala et al. 1984]. Drawing upon the ancient Indian concept of the thirty-two physical marks of a "Great Man" (*mahāpurisa*), the sutta begins by outlining the two potential destinies open to an individual possessing them: either becoming a wheel-turning universal monarch (*cakkavattin*) or a fully awakened Buddha [Cantwell 2010; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Anālayo 2017]. The discourse explains in detail how each bodily mark was karmically generated by the virtuous deeds and spiritual qualities perfected by Gautama as a bodhisattva in his previous lives [Cantwell 2010; Anālayo 2017]. For example, the wheel-marks on his feet are linked to his accomplishment of the four assemblies of disciples, while his smooth, dust-resistant skin is traced to his past habit of approaching ascetics and brahmins for instruction [Anālayo 2016]. Structurally, the text alternates between prose sections that examine the marks singly, in pairs, or in triads, and explanatory verse restatements introduced by quotation formulas such as *tatth' etaṃ vuccati* [Winternitz 1933; Dhammapala et al. 1984; Anālayo 2017].

Scholars note that the sutta contains some of the latest and most intricate verse forms in the Pali canon, including meters such as *vaṃsattha* [SuttaCentral; Sujato 2011; Sujato, History of Mindfulness]. While the Pali commentary attributes these explanatory verses to the elder Ānanda (*ānandattherena ṭhapitā vaṇṇanāgāthā*), their elaborate poetic style and omission from northern parallels indicate that they stem from a later devotional tradition, possibly added in Sri Lanka around the same period that extra material was added to the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* [Sujato 2011; Sujato 2012; Sujato, History of Mindfulness].

Full parallels are preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 59, *Discourse on the Thirty-two Marks*, likely of Sarvāstivāda provenance) and the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* (chapter 26), with partial parallels found in DN 33, DĀ 9, T 12, and Sanskrit fragments [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017]. DharmaNexus confirms these cross-language alignments with MĀ 59 (T 26) and the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, while also identifying extensive reuse in the Tibetan *Kāraṇaprajñapti* (D4087), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, *Daśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, *Mahāvadānasūtra*, and *Lalitavistara* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus identifies substantial shared passages with 192 texts, most notably the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* (DN 14), which shares standard descriptions of the thirty-two marks, as well as the *Cakkavatti Sutta* (DN 26), the *Sela Sutta* (MN 92 / Snp 3.7), the *Brahmāyu Sutta* (MN 91), and the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 4.7) [DharmaNexus].
